summary: Paul begins 'For this cause I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles' — and breaks off to explain his stewardship: the mystery made known to him by revelation, hidden from other generations, now revealed — that Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members, fellow partakers. He, 'the very least of all saints,' was given grace to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ and to make the mystery known — so that through the assembly God's manifold wisdom is being taught even to the principalities and powers. Then the sentence restarts: 'For this cause I bow my knees' — a prayer for inner strength, that Christ dwell in their hearts, that they grasp the width and length and height and depth, and know a love that surpasses knowledge, filled with all the fullness of God, to him who can do far more than all we ask or think.
whyItMatters: This chapter is the letter's hinge made personal: the cosmic mystery of chapters 1–2 turns out to run through one prisoner's commission, and the prayer that closes it asks for the one thing the whole letter needs — strength to grasp a love too large for knowledge. The doxology at the end is the summit of the letter's first half.

context.author: Paul, self-described twice: 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles' (3:1) and 'the very least of all saints' (3:8) — the steward of a grace he did not deserve.
context.audience: Gentile believers (3:1), who are themselves the content of the mystery Paul stewards — and who are asked not to lose heart at his troubles, 'which are your glory' (3:13).
context.date: Undated; the chapter's clock is God's — 'the eternal purpose which he accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord' (3:11).
context.setting: Written from prison (3:1); the chapter asks its readers to read his chains not as his shame but as part of their story.
context.literaryForm: A broken-and-resumed sentence (3:1-2, 3:14 — 'For this cause' twice) — Paul starts the prayer, stops to explain his commission, then bows his knees; the digression is the chapter's structure.

outline.heading: 'For this cause' — the prisoner's interruption
outline.note: Paul begins the prayer, then explains: the administration of God's grace given him, the mystery made known by revelation, written before in few words — that Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, fellow partakers of the promise; of this he was made a servant according to the gift of grace.

outline.heading: The least saint, the unsearchable riches
outline.note: To him, the very least of all saints, grace was given to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ and to bring to light the administration of the mystery hidden for ages in God — so that now, through the assembly, God's manifold wisdom is made known to the principalities and powers; therefore do not lose heart at his troubles, which are their glory.

outline.heading: 'For this cause' — the kneeling prayer
outline.note: The sentence restarts: bowing knees to the Father, from whom every family is named — strength through his Spirit in the inner person, Christ dwelling in their hearts through faith, rooted and grounded in love, strengthened to comprehend with all the saints the width, length, height, and depth, to know Christ's love surpassing knowledge, filled with all the fullness of God.

outline.heading: The doxology
outline.note: To him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us — to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

keyVerses.text: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of his promise in Christ Jesus through the Good News;
keyVerses.why: The mystery named in its sharpest form — three 'fellow' compounds in one sentence — the content everything else in the chapter serves.

keyVerses.text: to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places,
keyVerses.why: The letter's widest-angle claim about the assembly: its very existence is God's public lecture to the powers — a stage bigger than the congregation, bigger than the empire.

keyVerses.text: that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be strengthened to comprehend with all the saints what is the width and length and height and depth, and to know Christ’s love which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.
keyVerses.why: The prayer's summit — dimensions beyond measuring, a knowledge that outdoes knowledge, a filling that outdoes asking; the doxology that follows is the only fitting answer.

themes: glory to the one who does more

questions.question: Why does Paul interrupt himself in verse 1 and again in verse 14?
questions.answer: The chapter visibly breaks its own sentence: 'For this cause I, Paul, am the prisoner...' (3:1) stops before the prayer, resumes the commission explanation, then starts over — 'For this cause, I bow my knees' (3:14). The digression is the point: before he can pray for them, the letter must establish what his imprisonment has to do with them — the mystery he stewards is their own inclusion.

questions.question: What exactly is the 'mystery' in this chapter?
questions.answer: Named plainly at 3:6: 'the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of his promise in Christ Jesus through the Good News.' Hidden from other generations, now revealed to God's holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit (3:5). In this letter 'mystery' always means something once hidden, now disclosed — never an unsolved riddle.

questions.question: Why does Paul call himself 'the very least of all saints'?
questions.answer: The phrase intensifies his own earlier self-description — literally 'least' of all saints (3:8). It serves the argument: the mystery's magnitude is proved by the smallness of its messenger. Grace was given 'to me' the least to preach the unsearchable riches — the disproportion between the steward and the treasure is itself evidence that the treasure is God's, not man's.

questions.question: How is the assembly making God's wisdom known to 'principalities and powers'?
questions.answer: The claim at 3:10 is startling: through the assembly — this mixed, unimpressive congregation — God's manifold wisdom is right now being made known to the ranks the letter named in 1:21 and will name again in 6:12. The assembly is not the audience of the lesson but the instrument of it: that former enemies and strangers are one body displays a wisdom no power could have devised.

questions.question: Why does Paul say his troubles are 'your glory'?
questions.answer: 'Do not lose heart at my troubles for you, which are your glory' (3:13). His imprisonment is the price of the Gentile commission — the chain on his wrist exists because the mystery includes them. Reading it that way converts his suffering from scandal into evidence: the prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles (3:1) is the letter's own title for what his chains mean.

questions.question: What is the prayer in verses 14-19 asking for?
questions.answer: Strength, not new status: that God grant them, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person (3:16) — so that Christ dwells in their hearts through faith, they are rooted and grounded in love, and they are strengthened to comprehend the width, length, height, and depth, and to know Christ's love which surpasses knowledge, and so be filled with all the fullness of God (3:17-19). Everything asked is a deepening of what chapter 1 said they already have.

questions.question: What are 'the width and length and height and depth' of verse 18?
questions.answer: The letter gives the dimensions but not their object — and that is the verse's own design: 'strengthened to comprehend with all the saints' something measured in four directions. Most readers hear the dimensions of the love named in the next line ('to know Christ's love which surpasses knowledge'), some hear the whole plan of God, and the letter leaves the phrase open on purpose. The experience of grasping it is corporate — 'with all the saints.'

questions.question: Why does the chapter end in a doxology instead of a conclusion?
questions.answer: After a prayer whose last words are 'filled with all the fullness of God' (3:19), the only fitting move is praise: 'to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think' (3:20). The doxology closes the letter's first half — everything from 1:3 to here has been what God did, is doing, and can do — and its last words, 'to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations,' make the assembly's whole existence doxology.

questions.question: What does 'from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named' mean?
questions.answer: The line (3:15) is a wordplay in Greek: the Father (pater) is the source of every family (patria) — every household, every lineage, on earth and in heaven, derives its name and nature from him. In a letter about Jew and Gentile becoming one family, the prayer addresses the one Father from whom all the families come — the grounding of the letter's whole reconciliation theme.

glossary.def: The hosted text's word for oikonomia — a steward's management; Paul's commission to manage God's grace for the Gentiles (3:2, 3:9).
The mystery's sharpest claim: Gentiles share the inheritance, the body, and the promise as full partners — three 'fellow' words in one verse (3:6).
The many-colored wisdom of God (3:10) — displayed not in a book but in the assembly's existence, before an audience of powers.
